items.label: A
items.critique: Breathless exclamation-stacked plea, 'my sweet sister', the comma-less 'Hurry, kind sir and find a way out' and the bald 'tokens of my appreciation' handover are Westwood's plain, slightly clumsy cheer; the journal is a bare imperative.

items.label: B
items.critique: The plea is tidy and over-specified (pig farmer intro, cellar of the burned farmhouse, guards, key) in a measured cadence Westwood's panicked NPCs rarely have; the captive's 'Yaaaaaiiieeee!!' reads as an imitation of Nox's yelps bolted onto it.

items.label: C
items.critique: Many short fragments split across pages, the 'lost his eyebrows' joke and the captive's speechy 'bigger and braver than you' line feel crafted; the narrative journal with a trailing ellipsis is not how Nox phrases objectives.

items.label: D
items.critique: 'What took you so long to get here!?', 'Nox's vital interests', 'Charm or kill all the monsters... Rescue the 6 trapped mine workers' with a numeral, and the flat 'I'll follow you.' are exactly the campaign's functional voice and quest shape.

items.label: E
items.critique: The jammed express elevator, 'Chief Engineer', 'You'll make a fine [Group], lad' and the captive handing over a key and a secret passage are the campaign's logistics-heavy plainness with a cheerful mentor tone.

items.label: F
items.critique: 'beat him or eat him', 'a grim and terrible warning of my son's fate' and 'my courage holds -- lead me home!' are polished, rhythmic phrasing; the stew-warming reminder is a crafted character beat rather than Nox's blunt 'hurry' nag.

items.label: G
items.critique: The plea is pure world-building (salted fish, the lake rising) with no request or reward stated; the evenly measured, comma-correct sentences and the 'dry with my papa' callback read as a modern writer.

items.label: H
items.critique: Very short, blunt lines ('Help us!', 'Now be on your way!'), 'Well done, my boy!' and 'lovely women... damsels' have Westwood's dated, cheerful bluntness and a multi-group quest structure.

items.label: I
items.critique: Awkward constructions ('you're surely none of those rotten dead men', 'will even drain a bit of the boldest man's courage away', 'Here is my last apple, you have it') and the sentimental 'mend my heart' feel non-native and over-written; the reward line's 'better than you know' is a writerly flourish.

items.label: J
items.critique: The trapped frog, the grumpy 'Fine! I will follow you!' and the 'What's that you say? Loads and loads of money?' gag are Nox's goofy humour, delivered in short exclamation-heavy lines.

tells: Westwood's pleas are panicked and functional: exclamation marks, a stated reward ('I promise you a reward', 'reward you handsomely'), a key or item, and little scene description; the new texts spend the plea on setting detail (who the speaker is, what the place used to be) and sometimes never state the request or the reward.
Westwood's journal entries are bare imperatives, sometimes with numerals ('Rescue the 6 trapped mine workers'); a narrative journal with an ellipsis or editorial voice gives a new text away.

New texts reach for crafted turns of phrase and rhyme or rhythm ('beat him or eat him', 'my courage holds', 'mend my heart', 'grim and terrible warning'); Westwood's lines are flatter and plainer, with humour from situation and blunt asides (the frog, 'Loads and loads of money?') rather than polished quips.

Westwood's captives and followers say very little and generically ('I'll follow you.', 'Help us!', 'Hurry! Lead me to safety!'); the new texts give captives speechy, characterful lines addressed to the monsters.
Westwood's reminders are plain nags ('Time is running out. Now be on your way!'); new reminders tend to be character beats or odd aphorisms.
Westwood's punctuation is looser (missing commas before 'and', '!?', '?!', double dashes for asides); the new texts are more grammatically tidy, or else awkward in a non-native way.
